title: Set Up Each Object
content:
What problem does this solve?
Assigning every attribute manually after object creation is repetitive. Python calls `__init__` when a new instance is created so the object can be set up immediately.

Store constructor inputs
  class Player:
      def __init__(self, name, score):
          self.name = name
          self.score = score
`name` and `score` are local parameters for this call. `self.name` and `self.score` are attributes stored on the particular instance.

self means this instance
When `Player("Ada", 3)` creates an object, that object is the value received by the method's `self` parameter. self is conventional Python naming, not a magic global variable.

Fresh mutable state per instance
If each object needs its own list, create `self.inventory = []` inside `__init__`. Since __init__ runs for every new object, each instance receives a fresh list.

Vocabulary after the behavior
Initialization is the setup performed for a new object. `__init__` is the initialization method; self is the parameter referring to the instance receiving that method call.
concepts: Python calls __init__ during ordinary ClassName(...) construction
self is the instance receiving the method call
Constructor parameters are local names; self attributes remain stored on the object
self.name = name stores an input on this instance
Fresh mutable per-instance state should be created inside __init__

examples.title: Automatic setup
examples.explanation: The constructor arguments become stored instance attributes.

examples.title: Two separate instances
examples.code:
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
a = Player("Ada")
b = Player("Bo")
print(a.name)
print(b.name)
examples.explanation: The same setup method stores different values on different instances.

examples.title: Fresh list per instance
examples.explanation: The list expression runs for every new Bag, so each object gets its own list.

common_mistakes: Forgetting self in the method parameter list
Writing name = name instead of self.name = name
Thinking self is magic rather than the instance parameter
Creating a mutable class-level list when each instance needs its own
Calling __init__ directly instead of using normal construction

exercises.title: Constructor arguments become attributes
hints: The value Ada is passed into the name parameter during construction.
self.name stores that value on p.
p.name therefore prints Ada.

exercises.title: Store the attribute
exercises.prompt: Complete the constructor assignment so the new Player stores its name.
hints: The right side is the local constructor parameter.
The left side must be the attribute on this instance.
Use `self.name = name`.

exercises.title: Store two attributes
exercises.prompt: Complete Player so `Player(name, score)` stores both `self.name` and `self.score`.
hints: Each constructor input should be saved on the particular instance.
Use two self attributes, one for each parameter.
Assign `self.name = name` and `self.score = score`.

exercises.title: Two separate instances
exercises.code_to_predict:
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
a = Player("Ada")
b = Player("Bo")
a.name = "Changed"
print(b.name)
hints: Construction created two separate instances.
Changing an attribute on a changes a only.
b.name remains Bo.

exercises.title: Where should the list be created?
exercises.prompt: Every Character needs a separate inventory. Which design matches that requirement?
choices: One class attribute: `inventory = []` shared by all instances.
Inside `__init__`: `self.inventory = []` so every construction creates a fresh list.
hints: Recall the shared-reference lesson: one list object shared by every instance is not independent state.
__init__ runs each time a new object is constructed.
Create `self.inventory = []` inside __init__.

exercises.title: Missing self
exercises.prompt: Repair the constructor so it accepts the instance parameter and stores the provided name on that instance.
hints: The initialization method needs both the instance and the caller-provided name.
Add self as the first parameter, then store the local name parameter on self.
Use `def __init__(self, name): self.name = name`.

exercises.title: Shared inventory
exercises.prompt: Both characters currently share one class-level inventory. Move inventory creation into per-instance setup so each Character has its own list.
hints: The problem is that the list is created once on the class instead of once per object.
Move the list expression into __init__ and store it through self.
Remove the class-level list and add `self.inventory = []` inside __init__.

tests.expression: (lambda pair: pair[0].inventory is not pair[1].inventory)([Character("A"), Character("B")])

exercises.title: Local name or stored attribute?
exercises.prompt: In `def __init__(self, name): self.name = name`, which statement is correct?
choices: Both occurrences of name are global variables.
The parameter `name` is local to the constructor call; `self.name` is the attribute that remains stored on the instance.
self.name disappears when the constructor returns.
hints: Use what you learned about function scope.
The bare parameter name belongs to this method call; the dotted attribute belongs to the object.
The local parameter disappears after the call, but self.name remains on the instance.

exercises.title: Character Setup
exercises.prompt: Define `Character(name, health)` storing name and health and creating a fresh empty inventory for every instance. Hidden checks will construct several characters and mutate one inventory to prove the state is independent.
hints: Turn the repeated post-construction setup from Lesson 25 into one __init__ method.
Store both inputs through self and create the inventory list inside __init__.
Define `__init__(self, name, health)` with self.name, self.health, and `self.inventory = []`.

tests.expression: (lambda pair: pair[0].inventory is not pair[1].inventory)([Character("Aria",10), Character("Rook",14)])

exercises.success_message: Construction now produces fully initialized characters with fresh mutable state per instance.
